data.title: Week Ahead for FX, Bonds: U.S. Midterms, Jobs Data in Focus; BOE Expected to Raise Rates
data.description:
By Dow Jones Newswires staff 




  Below are the most important global events likely to affect FX and bond markets in the week starting Nov. 2. 



  The U.S. midterm elections will likely take center stage in the week, while the latest monthly U.S. jobs data could give clues on how soon the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again. 



  The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates, while rate decisions are also due in Sweden, Norway, Brazil and Mexico. 



  In Asia, central bank decisions in Australia and Malaysia will take center stage, with the Reserve Bank of Australia widely expected to raise interest rates for a fifth time this year. Bank Negara Malaysia is expected to hold rates steady. 





  U.S. 





  The U.S. midterm elections are due on Tuesday. The results of these will be closely watched by investors as Democrats are expected to perform well, with potential consequences for policy going forward. Democrats are widely expected to secure control of the House, while there's a possibility that the party also takes control of the Senate. 



  "A Democratic sweep...could be seen as slightly negative for the U.S. dollar from a few angles, from higher risk of government shutdown and gridlock on debt ceiling negotiations to potential damage to already shaky AI-related sentiment," ING foreign exchange strategist Francesco Pesole said in a note. 



  U.S. jobs data will also be in focus, particularly the latest nonfarm payrolls report for October, due on Friday, as investors gauge the likely timing and pace of future interest-rate rises based on evidence regarding the strength of the U.S. economy. 



  The Federal Reserve left interest rates on hold at its recent meeting but most analysts expect rates will rise in December. U.S. money markets price a 76% probability of a quarter-point rate hike on Dec. 9 and fully price at least two increases within the next 12 months, LSEG data showed. Job creation might have to be particularly weak for investors to meaningfully change these expectations. 



  "We expect sluggish employment growth and a stable unemployment rate," analysts at LBBW said in a note. Despite this, a 25-basis-point interest-rate hike by the Fed on Dec. 9 "is still considered very likely," they said. 



  Ahead of Friday's jobs data, further indications on the health of the U.S. jobs market will come with U.S. JOLTS job opening figures for September on Tuesday, ADP private payrolls data for October on Wednesday and weekly jobless claims Thursday. 



  The ISM surveys for October on manufacturing on Monday and services on Wednesday, followed by the University of Michigan's preliminary November consumer sentiment survey on Friday, will provide a more up-to-date picture of how the U.S. economy is faring. 





  Canada 





  Canadian jobs data for October are due Friday. These will give a picture of the health of Canada's economy after the Bank of Canada recently raised interest rates by 25 basis points. 



  Money markets price a 55% chance of a back-to-back increase in December, LSEG data showed. 



  Nick Rees, head of macro research at Monex, expects that underlying inflation is too soft and the labor market too weak to justify another hike, he said in a note. 





  Latin America 





  Brazil's central bank will announce its policy decision on Wednesday in the wake of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's surprise election victory. 



  "We expect Banco Central do Brasil to pause at its meeting on November 4 to gauge the inflation impact of the market sell-off triggered by Brazil's presidential election," Standard Chartered economist Dan Pan said in a note. 



  If sharp depreciation of the Brazilian real is sustained, it will likely raise near-term inflation pressure, the analyst said. The loose fiscal stance expected during Lula's fourth term might lead to a further increase in long-term inflation expectations, Pan said. Nevertheless, there is unlikely to be a sharp enough fiscal deterioration to push BCB back to raising rates, the analyst added. 



  Mexico's central bank, or Banxico, announces a rate decision on Thursday, and is expected to leave its key rate at 6.50%. 



  "Since the September meeting, the case for additional easing has weakened. Recent activity indicators suggest a faster closing of the output gap, the currency depreciated, while core inflation has recently re-accelerated," Citi analysts said in a note. 





  Eurozone 





  Eurozone provisional inflation data for October due on Wednesday will be the most closely-watched eurozone indicator of the week. This comes after the European Central Bank left interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, with money markets pricing a 63% probability of a quarter-point rate hike in December, LSEG data showed. 



  Investec forecasts that eurozone headline annual inflation will rise to 3.9% and reach 4.0% by the end of the year. LBBW analysts expect it will have hit 4.0% already in October. 



  The inflation data will be an important indicator for the ECB, Investec economist Ryan Djajasaputra said in a note. ECB President Christine Lagarde said the central bank had debated a hike in October and it is therefore likely gearing up towards more tightening in December, he said. 



  Final October manufacturing purchasing managers' surveys for France, Germany and the eurozone will be released Monday, followed by the equivalent surveys for services activity on Wednesday. 



  German September manufacturing orders are released Thursday, alongside French September industrial production figures and eurozone PPI inflation, also for September. 



  Eurozone September retail sales and German September industrial production data are due Friday. 





  U.K. 





  The main event in the week will be the Bank of England interest rate decision on Thursday, where markets widely expect the central bank to increase interest rates by 25 basis points to 4.0%. 



  "[The BOE] will deliver a required tightening that had already become clear at the prior meeting," Allan Monks, a senior economist at J.P. Morgan, said in a note. 



  Nonetheless, analysts expect the BOE to push back against current market expectations for more than four rate hikes over the coming 12 months, given that there is little evidence of second-order inflation effects yet. 



  "There is a high bar for the BOE to deliver tightening in line with market pricing," BNP Paribas economist Dani Stoilova said in a note. 



  The final U.K. manufacturing purchasing managers' index data for October will be released Monday, followed by the final services purchasing managers' figures on Wednesday. 





  Scandinavia 





  Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, will announce a policy decision on Wednesday. Markets price an 87% chance of a 25 basis points rate increase to 1.75%, LSEG data showed. 



  The central bank left rates on hold last month but signaled it could raise rates later this year. 



  The Riksbank faces an improved growth outlook, Bank of America analysts said in a note. With data doing little to challenge the Riksbank's indication of future tightening, "we continue to expect a hike...and another one in the first quarter of 2027," they said. 



  Norway's Norges Bank will announce an interest-rate decision on Thursday. 



  At its last meeting in September, Norway's central bank raised rates by 25 basis points. It is likely to leave its policy rate unchanged at 4.50% on Thursday and signal that rates will remain elevated for some time, Nomura analysts said in a note. 



  "Although underlying inflation remains too high, we expect it to slow in the coming months." The current policy rate is restrictive, putting dampening pressure on inflation, they said. 





  Central and Eastern Europe 





  The National Bank of Poland announces a policy decision on Wednesday. Headline inflation has been running above the central bank's target in recent months but there is little evidence of broader price pressures building, affording the NBP time to respond, ING analysts said in a note. 



  "Our baseline scenario assumes that NBP rates would remain unchanged through the end of this year." Two rate rises in the first quarter of 2027 are possible if the energy price shock continues and inflation remains elevated, they said. 



  The Czech National Bank's policy decision is on Thursday, with markets pricing an 84% chance that the central bank will raise interest rates by 25 basis points to 4.0%, LSEG data showed. 



  Headline and core inflation have exceeded the central bank's forecasts, while accelerating wages and higher energy and food prices point to further price pressures, ING analysts said in a note. 



  "The combination of persistent inflation pressures and robust consumption should keep further monetary tightening on the agenda, with the December and February meetings potentially in play depending on incoming inflation data." 





  Japan 





  Japan's monetary policy outlook will remain in focus in the week, with investors looking for clues on the Bank of Japan's next interest-rate increase after the central bank held rates steady at 1.25% in its October meeting, while signaling that further tightening remains possible. 



  On Thursday, the Bank of Japan is scheduled to release the minutes of its September meeting, at which it raised interest rates by 25 basis points to 1.25% to keep persistent inflation in check. 



  The Ministry of Finance is slated to auction 10-year government bonds Thursday, testing investor demand as markets assess the prospect of higher borrowing costs. 



  Japanese markets will be closed Tuesday for the Culture Day holiday. 





  China 





  A quiet data week is in store for China, with PMIs the primary indicator of note. 



  On Monday and Wednesday, private gauges of China's manufacturing and services sector activity are due. The RatingDog PMIs compiled by S&P Global, which survey more export-oriented businesses, are likely to keep outperforming official counterparts. 



  (MORE TO FOLLOW) Dow Jones Newswires



  October 30, 2026 13:08 ET (17:08 GMT)

data.title: Week Ahead for FX, Bonds: U.S. Midterms, Jobs -2-
data.description:
The PMIs are closely watched as forward-looking indicators of economic performance, capturing sentiment among businesses and demand trends. A robust reading would underscore views that the world's second-largest economy remains resilient despite headwinds from trade frictions and the energy shock.

Foreign-exchange reserves figures from the central bank will also be in focus. 




  Australia 





  The week ahead in Australia will be dominated by the Reserve Bank of Australia, which holds its policy meeting Monday and Tuesday. 



  The overwhelming consensus is for the central bank to raise interest rates for a fifth time this year while keeping the door open to further tightening. 



  The RBA is battling persistent inflation despite aggressively raising interest rates this year, and is increasingly concerned that expectations of higher inflation could become entrenched. Economists say they aren't ruling out another rate increase in December or February, given the RBA's hawkish rhetoric in recent months. 



  To prevent inflation expectations from rising further, the central bank may opt for more short-term economic pain to curb demand and bring inflation back to target. With interest rates already at their highest level in 15 years and house prices falling at the fastest pace in decades, another rate increase could further weigh on already weak consumer confidence in the final months of the year. 



  RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser, who has recently been outspoken about the risks of higher inflation, is scheduled to speak Thursday. His comments could offer clues about the outlook for the December policy meeting. 





  Asia PMIs 





  A slew of monthly manufacturing PMI readings for Asia are due on Monday, including Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Southeast Asia. The surveys will be closely watched as cost pressures and higher rates could weigh on business confidence and operating conditions. 



  Flash PMI data showed that business activity is diverging across different markets as geopolitical and macroeconomic conditions affect the private sector and inflation to various extents. 





  South Korea 





  South Korea is scheduled to release its October trade data Sunday, Nov. 1, and inflation figures Tuesday, Nov. 3. Economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal expect export growth to have accelerated, while consumer inflation likely eased slightly. 



  The median forecast from a WSJ poll of 11 economists is for an 86.7% increase in exports from a year earlier, compared with a revised 83.7% rise in September. Imports are projected to have risen 38.1%, resulting in a $38.28 billion trade surplus in October, compared with the previous month's revised $49.97 billion surplus, the poll showed. 



  "Strong export momentum has continued, supported by more working days than in October last year and sustained strength in semiconductor exports," said iM Securities chief economist Park Sang-hyun. 



  The median forecast from a separate WSJ poll of nine economists is for consumer prices to have risen 2.8% from a year earlier, slowing from September's 2.9% increase. On a monthly basis, prices likely edged up 0.2% in October after rising 0.3% in September, the poll showed. 



  Mild weather following the Chuseok holiday likely helped stabilize agricultural prices, while a stronger won may have eased upward pressure on import prices, Meritz Securities chief economist Seunghoon Stephen Lee said. 





  Hong Kong 





  Hong Kong is set to release advance third-quarter GDP figures and September retail sales data Tuesday. The city's economy has shown resilience this year, expanding 4.3% from a year earlier in the second quarter. 



  Citi expects third-quarter GDP growth of 3.5% from a year earlier, supported by AI-related merchandise trade and stronger investment. However, modest consumption growth could lead to a slight contraction of 0.3% from the previous quarter, its economists said. 





  Southeast Asia 





  Inflation will be in focus across Southeast Asia during the week, with rising energy and food prices expected to push up consumer prices in the region. 



  In the Philippines, headline inflation likely accelerated to 8.4% in October from 7.2% in September, according to ANZ Research. Crude-oil prices reached a six-month high by the end of October, likely keeping domestic fuel prices elevated. 



  Thailand's headline inflation is also expected to rise sharply, with Barclays forecasting a 3.5% increase in October, up from 2.82% in September, driven by higher energy and food prices. The Bank of Thailand expects inflation to continue rising into early 2027 due to higher energy costs and the effects of El Nino. 



  Indonesia's October inflation is expected to edge up to 3.4% from 3.3% in September, driven largely by higher food prices, ANZ said. Meanwhile, Indonesia's September trade surplus likely narrowed as rising crude-oil prices pushed up import costs, according to Barclays. 



  The nation's growth print for the third quarter is expected to ease to 5.2% from 5.3% in the previous quarter as weaker consumer spending weighed on activity, partly offset by government support for lower-income households, according to DBS. 





  Malaysia 





  Bank Negara Malaysia is expected to keep its overnight policy rate unchanged at 2.75% at its November meeting, although the risk of a 25-basis-point hike remains, Citi analysts said. 



  Stronger-than-expected third quarter growth, rising producer prices and wage pressures, alongside Budget 2027 measures, could prompt an earlier rate increase, they say. Citi now expects a 25 basis point hike in January 2027, but a stronger signal at the November meeting remains possible as inflation risks persist. 





  Taiwan 





  Taiwan is due to release its October inflation data on Thursday. The island's consumer prices likely remained elevated, with economists' estimates ranging from 2.3% to 2.7% growth. Higher global energy costs fed into higher electricity prices, and airfare prices and services inflation remained sticky, DBS economists said. 



  The odds for Taiwan's central bank to deliver its first interest rate hike in December after standing pat for 10 consecutive quarters are rising. Goldman Sachs economists expect it to deliver three consecutive quarterly rate increases of 12.5 basis points each starting in December. The economists expect this tightening cycle to be short, however, given prospects of a brief Fed tightening cycle followed by a potential resumption of rate cuts in the second half of 2027. 





  Any references to days are in local times.

data.title: GRUNGE: The Noise is Coming Back!
data.description:
GRUNGE: The Noise is Coming Back!

GRUNGE: The Noise is Coming Back!

PR Newswire

TUCSON, Ariz., Oct. 30, 2026

TUCSON, Ariz., Oct. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- GRUNGE is a feature-length suspense horror-thriller born from the collision between Seattle's grunge Legacy and the underground music culture, mythology, and psychedelic horror.

Set in 1993, the story focuses on a popular grunge band.  But it isn't a nostalgic recreation of the 1990s. Rather, it's a horror film using the mythology of grunge as its cultural foundation. The film combines the raw energy of the grunge music culture with a genuinely terrifying set of circumstances ... something simultaneously familiar and dangerous—a story rooted in recognizable cultural history that gets pushed into psychedelic, psychological, and visceral horror.

A rising rock band is on the verge of stardom, with a scorching new single lighting up the airwaves and their debut music video premiering on MTV. Everything seems to be falling into place, when disaster strikes. Following a sudden and tragic turn of events, the band is thrust into a violent psychedelic spiral, leading them down a blood-soaked path of death and destruction,

Based on a story by Rene Rivas with special effects by Quin Davis, the 15-minute short film premieres on Crypt TV on Halloween Eve, October 30, 2026. (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8pcHB-sEGvc).  The goal of this 'proof of concept' short version is to ignite audience interest, turning that audience into a community that will help bring the full feature version to life. 

Rene Rivas is an independent filmmaker, writer, producer, director, and cinematographer based in Tucson, Arizona, who has spent years developing independent narrative and genre projects, with a particular interest in creating ambitious films outside the traditional studio system.

Quin Davis is a sought-after Special FX expert whose work has appeared in productions by major studios, including Paramount, Sony, Universal, and Columbia.  His company, Davis FX, is also based in Tucson.  

The film will be shot in Tucson in March 2027.

An official Indiegogo campaign for the GRUNGE feature film will launch when the short film premiers on Crypt TV.  The coordinated release gives audiences an immediate opportunity to watch the proof of concept, experience the world of the film, and participate directly in helping create the feature. The film already has in-kind services partnership with Movie Maker Magazine. For an independently financed feature, that is significant.

Launching a feature-film crowdfunding campaign in conjunction with Crypt TV is a first-of-its-kind collaboration – a direct bridge between a short-form proof of concept and a feature-film campaign.  The strategy is designed to create a single, concentrated moment in which the film's release and its next stage of development become one event.

One of the project's most significant music-world connections comes through Daniel House, whose history is deeply intertwined with the Seattle scene that gave birth to grunge. House was a central figure behind C/Z Records, the influential Seattle label that released early recordings from artists who would become foundational figures in the grunge movement, including Nirvana, Soundgarden, and Green River, among others. His involvement gives GRUNGE a connection to the actual musical history behind the mythology. 

This isn't a film simply using grunge as an aesthetic. GRUNGE is also receiving support from Sub Pop, the legendary Seattle-based label whose history is inseparable from the emergence of grunge into the international cultural consciousness.  The relationship further connects the project to the musical ecosystem that helped define the genre. Together, the involvement of C/Z Records and Sub Pop gives GRUNGE something particularly valuable: AUTHENTICITY.

data.title: After Intel's historic stock drop, analysts say there's no reason to buy the dip
data.description:
By Britney Nguyen

'A cheaper stock does not necessarily offer better value,' one expert says

Intel, led by CEO Lip-Bu Tan, disappointed investors with its latest forecast.

Even in the wake of what could be Intel's worst daily stock drop in decades, some analysts say investors should steer clear.

"A cheaper stock does not necessarily offer better value," Dan Kemp, founder of investment consultancy Portfolio Thinking, told MarketWatch.

Intel's (INTC) earnings report on Thursday afternoon shed light on various problems, including a dramatically weakening market for personal-computer chips and a server business that's leaving money on the table because it can't meet all its demand. Intel is also losing money on an expensive chip-manufacturing business that remains a work in progress.

Seaport Research analyst Jay Goldberg thinks that Intel "will sort itself out" eventually, but its comeback "is taking too long."

The company's current challenges, which partly stem from poor foresight into market conditions that has left the company without enough manufacturing capacity for its critical AI server chips, have put a dent in the turnaround efforts undertaken by CEO Lip-Bu Tan.

Goldberg, who just lowered his rating on Intel to neutral from buy, said he sees "no reason to own the stock" as the company works through its issues.

Intel's 29% stock drop as of midday Friday puts it on pace for its worst one-day decline since at least 1980, according to Dow Jones Market Data. It also draws flashbacks to August 2024, when Intel shares shed 26% in a single day upon suspending its dividend and beginning a massive cost-cutting program.

To the company's credit, Intel is in better shape than it was two years ago, Goldberg said. Its chip-manufacturing technology is gaining traction with customers and producing better yields, he said, referring to the amount of usable chips that come from a single wafer. The commentary around its chip-manufacturing business "gives us further confidence that Intel Foundry will be viable, some day," Goldberg said in a note to clients.

That prospect alone may not be reason to buy into Intel's stock now, however.

Intel on Thursday said that persistent weakness in demand for PCs, spurred by rising memory prices, was partly to blame for a forecast that came short of what analysts had been expecting.

There are also constraints throughout its supply chain, the company noted, including for chip wafers and packaging substrates - an essential component for its advanced chip packaging technology that is gaining appeal with customers.

Intel had indicated the previous quarter it was getting back on track with supply, Goldberg said - but the third-quarter results showed that hasn't happened.

While Intel has upped production of client wafers for the PC market, which "is seeing its worst downturn" in more than a decade, it is facing shortages of wafers for data-center server central processing units to support an artificial-intelligence market that "is seeing its greatest cycle ever," he noted.

"Where they really lost us was management's commentary that supply would not come into balance until the middle of next year," he said, also noting that Intel said its investments in long-term assets to benefit the business could weigh on its cash flow, or the money it generates after that spending and operating expenses.

Don't miss: AMD's stock slides after Intel earnings reveal two big issues

Although the stock's steep drop on Friday follows its less-than-stellar report, it also has to do with investors realizing "the size of the mountain Intel must climb over the next decade to justify its previous valuation," Portfolio Thinking's Kemp said.

At Intel's current valuation, the market needs Intel Foundry to bring in $14 billion a year, Kemp said - a high mark for a business that has lost money for several consecutive quarters and generated external revenue of just $411 million in the September quarter.

While the selloff could look like a bargain to some investors, Kemp said its important to distinguish between that and a discount.

Indeed, Intel shares now trade at 35.9x estimated forward earnings, down from 43.8x heading into the report on Thursday, according to Dow Jones Market Data. But the earnings also made investors call into question trends like its ability to capitalize appropriately on a wave of demand for server CPUs, something that had previously helped drive its valuation higher.

Richard Windsor, founder of research firm Radio Free Mobile, shared similar caution about the stock given his view that while Tan has made progress on a turnaround, "he is not out of the woods yet."

The stock's high valuation, Intel's weak projections for next year and the ongoing debate over the dominance of its x86 chip architecture "leaves me cautious on the shares," Windsor said in a note to clients.

Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya also lowered his rating on Intel's stock to neutral from a previous buy position.

Intel's PC weakness "more than" offsets the strength it is showing in its data-center and AI segment, Arya said in a note to clients.

And even as it benefits from AI-driven demand for server CPUs, Intel faces component-supply issues there, while its offerings "are not yet technically competitive" with those from CPU rivals Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Arm (ARM), according to Arya.

-Britney Nguyen

data.title: Fed's Musalem: Additional Firming of Monetary Policy Will Be Necessary, and Soon
data.description:
By Jessica Coacci 




  St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said additional firming of monetary policy will be necessary, and soon after the central bank held interest rates steady this week. 



  Speaking at an event in New York Friday, Musalem said that incremental adjustments to policy made earlier are usually less disruptive than larger, and abrupt actions taken later. The Fed kept interest rates unchanged Wednesday. Market participants project a 76% chance of a rate increase in December, according to CME's FedWatch tool. 



  "Moving sooner in smaller steps while inflation expectations are anchored has a better chance of succeeding without adverse impact on the labor market or economic growth" a published text of his remarks said. 



  Musalem also said he is focused on two plausible inflation scenarios in the next 18 months. 



  In the scenario he deems as more likely, persistent strong demand and ongoing supply pressures keep inflation elevated absent additional firming of policy. 



  Musalem also said he agrees with Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's characterization of the recent increase in the FOMC policy rate last month as "removing a dose of accommodation." Musalem said policy remains accommodative, and further firming will likely be necessary to ensure inflation converges to 2% in a timely manner. 



  Under the less likely but still plausible scenario, Musalem says, falling energy prices and lower shipping costs, or an increase in potential output growth driven by higher productivity growth, might ease inflation pressures. Under this second scenario, additional policy firming would not be required. 



  "Alternatively, aggregate demand might slow more than is now expected, perhaps because spending on AI or data centers slows substantially, or financial conditions tighten abruptly and wealth effects driven consumption spending decelerate," he said. 



  Musalem said that because he views the second scenario less likely than the first, a further removal of monetary policy accommodation will be required to ensure inflation converges to 2% within 18 months. 





  Write to Jessica Coacci at jessica.coacci@wsj.com 





  (END) Dow Jones Newswires

Commerce Bancshares, Inc. Declares Stock Dividend and Quarterly Cash Dividend on Common Stock

Commerce Bancshares, Inc. (NASDAQ: CBSH) announced today that its Board of Directors declared a quarterly dividend of $0.275 per share on the Company's common stock. The dividend is payable on December 21, 2026 to stockholders of record at the close of business on December 1, 2026.

The Board of Directors also approved a 5% common stock dividend payable on December 22, 2026 to shareholders of record at the close of business on December 1, 2026. Statements reflecting the issuance of shares as a result of the stock dividend should be mailed on or about December 22, 2026. No fractional shares will be issued, and shareholders will receive cash for such fractional interests based on the market value of the stock on the record date. The quarterly cash dividend will not be payable on any shares to be issued pursuant to the 5% stock dividend.

About Commerce Bancshares, Inc.

Commerce Bancshares, Inc. (NASDAQ: CBSH) is a regional bank holding company with $34.8 billion in assets¹, offering banking, payment solutions, wealth management and securities brokerage through its subsidiaries. Commerce Bank, its primary subsidiary, brings over 160 years of experience helping individuals and businesses through high-touch service and sophisticated, personalized financial solutions.

Commerce maintains an extensive network of banking centers, wealth offices, and ATMs throughout the Midwest, as well as commercial offices in 11 states and offers payment solutions nationwide. The company also delivers financial planning, private banking, investment management and trust services to clients through a network of dedicated wealth offices across the country. Customers can conveniently access their accounts 24/7 using mobile and online platforms, as well as a customer service line.

Learn more at www.commercebank.com

data.title: Trump administration is illegally delaying student-debt forgiveness for tens of thousands of public servants, lawsuit alleges
data.description:
By Jillian Berman

Teachers, nurses and other borrowers have waited years for approval to complete their payment obligation and access debt relief, the suit claims

The Education Department, lead by Linda McMahon, is stalling progress toward student-debt forgiveness for public servants, a lawsuit alleges.

The Trump administration is stalling access to student-debt relief for tens of thousands of public servants who are entitled to it, a class-action lawsuit filed in federal court Friday by the American Federation of Teachers and several student-loan borrowers alleges.

Borrowers in the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, an initiative that allows people who have been working for the government and certain nonprofits for 10 years to have their federal student loans canceled, are struggling to get answers about when they'll qualify for promised debt relief, according to the suit.

In order to have their debt wiped out, people working in public-service jobs must make 120 monthly payments. The complaint alleges that according to the most recent data available, which is from April of this year, 88,000 borrowers who have applied to make several of their final payments in a lump sum were waiting for an answer from the Education Department about whether they'll be able to do so.

That limbo, which for some of the named plaintiffs has lasted more than a year, has prevented them from moving forward in other ways in their financial lives, attorneys for the borrowers say. If they give up on waiting for an answer from the government and instead move forward with making their final payments through the regular process, many of them could wind up paying thousands of dollars more on their loans than if the Education Department approved their application to make the lump-sum payments, the suit claims.

Some people in public-service jobs are also seeing months of payments that had previously been counted toward the 120 needed for forgiveness disappear from their student-loan accounts, the suit alleges. Overall, the complaint paints a picture of a system sowing confusion and unease for nurses, teachers and other borrowers, many of whom have been working in public-service jobs and paying their loans for years.

The wait for answers "makes it extremely difficult for people to make any kinds of financial plans for their future," said Laura Dismore, senior counsel at the advocacy group Protect Borrowers and one of the attorneys representing the borrowers. "People are putting off starting families, people are putting off changing jobs or changing careers. Borrowers talk about intense stress and anxiety around not knowing when in some cases a six-figure debt is going to be forgiven."

The issues these borrowers are allegedly facing come as the Trump administration is in the midst of overhauling the student-loan system. Officials are implementing new repayment plans, getting rid of old ones and reportedly preparing to restart debt collection on defaulted student loans. Meanwhile, the Education Department currently has about half the staff it had in previous years. With all of these changes, borrowers have complained that they have struggled to obtain basic information about their loans and to get paperwork processed in a timely fashion.

In addition to these logistical challenges, advocates have worried about the Trump administration's philosophical approach to PSLF. Earlier this year, several organizations sued the Education Department after it said it would cut off access to PSLF for people employed at organizations that work on issues, such as immigration and gender-related healthcare for minors, that are in the administration's ideological crosshairs. The Trump administration recently backed down from defending the policy in court.

"They seem determined not to help those to have dedicated their careers to public service, but to hurt them," AFT President Randi Weingarten said of the Trump administration in comments to reporters.

The Education Department didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.

Waiting years for an answer to whether they'll get debt relief

Ever since borrowers could start claiming forgiveness under PSLF in 2017, the program has been plagued by challenges and confusion. The first year borrowers could apply for forgiveness under the program, 99% of those who applied were rejected, in large part because they didn't have the right type of federal student loan or weren't in the right repayment plan.

In the ensuing years, borrowers found themselves losing out on months of eligibility because they were put in forbearance - a payment pause - by their servicer, either because they made their payments too early or for other reasons.

Under the Biden administration, officials made changes aimed at cleaning up some of the sticking points for borrowers. One of those efforts, known as the buyback program, is a major focus of the lawsuit. In 2022, the Education Department launched an initiative that allowed borrowers who had spent months in forbearance but were still working for an employer that qualified them for PSLF to "buy back" those months. Previously, any months spent in forbearance didn't count toward the 120 needed for a borrower to have their debt canceled under the program.

To be eligible for the buyback program, the months spent in forbearance have to bring the borrower to the 120 needed to qualify for relief. For example, a borrower who spent five months in forbearance can apply for a buyback once they have made 115 payments.

To obtain the buyback, the borrower fills out a form and sends it to the Education Department. They need to be able to pay the full amount of the missed months within 90 days of the date on the buyback agreement.

The Education Department evaluates these applications, but the suit alleges that the department has essentially stalled on doing that. The last time the department released the numbers on how many buyback applications were still pending, in April, there were 88,000, according to the suit.

"We have borrowers who have been waiting two years at this point for their buyback applications to be processed," Dismore said. She added that they've learned recently that some newer applications have been processed, but there "doesn't appear to be any rhyme or reason to the order they are processing these applications."

Being stuck in this backlog has real consequences for borrowers, the suit claims.

One of the named plaintiffs, David Petley, works at a rural community hospital as a pharmacist and owes $338,000 on his loans, according to the suit. He has 11 years of employment that qualify for PSLF. He was placed in an involuntary forbearance that lost him eight months of progress toward PSLF, the suit claims. Petley filed two buyback applications in May 2025, according to the suit.

The suit alleges that he hasn't heard back from the Education Department on the status of his buyback applications except through the office of his member of Congress, who said the department confirmed it had received at least one buyback application, and that it was still pending.

"Despite a congressional inquiry on my behalf, the Department of Education has not told me where my application stands in the queue and nor have they provided me with an estimated timeline," Petley told reporters. "We are ready to settle up, but we have no clear answer about when that might happen."

If Petley decides to pay the last eight months of his loan instead of waiting for an answer on his buyback application, he'll have to pay $23,500 for those months, instead of the less than $15,000 he would pay through the buyback program, according to the suit. In some cases like his, the amount borrowers would have to pay now is higher than what they would pay under the buyback program because cheaper repayment plans that existed when they were in forbearance have disappeared, or because they are paying on plans tied to their income, which has gone up in the ensuing years.

Petley said that he took a pay cut when he decided to work at a nonprofit hospital in rural Oregon, but the promise of eventual debt relief made the move financially manageable.

"Public-service loan forgiveness helped draw me to work at a rural hospital," he said. "That's evidence of this program working. But for professionals considering the same path, the promise has to be dependable."

Progress toward debt forgiveness is clawed back

The suit highlights other challenges with the PSLF program that are plaguing borrowers. According to the complaint, borrowers are seeing months of payments that their accounts once showed counted toward PSLF disappear.

Elizabeth Schoepflin is one of those borrowers, the suit alleges. She has worked as a speech pathologist in a New York school for roughly 16 years. The suit claims that earlier this year, she had made 119 qualifying payments and was on track to make her 120th payment in April. That month, she made her 120th payment and submitted the final form certifying that her employment qualifies for PSLF, the suit says.

She waited months to see her loan balance disappear, but she wasn't alarmed, because she had experienced delays with the Education Department and its servicers' handling of PSLF paperwork before, the suit claims. Then in August, she received notice from the department that she was losing credit for the payments she made from February 2025 to April 2026, even though she was working at the same job and made payments on the same plan during that period as she had in previous years when her payments counted, according to the suit.

Now the department says she needs 15 more payments to get her $43,000 in student debt canceled, but it has provided no explanation for the change, the lawsuit alleges.

data.title: Marathon Runners Take to the Big Apple to Raise Awareness of Liver Disease
data.description:
Marathon Runners Take to the Big Apple to Raise Awareness of Liver Disease

Marathon Runners Take to the Big Apple to Raise Awareness of Liver Disease

PR Newswire

NEW YORK, Oct. 30, 2026

2026 TCS New York City Marathon is Sunday, November 1st

NEW YORK, Oct. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- American Liver Foundation (ALF) is proud to once again be a member of the TCS New York City Marathon Charity Program, for the 2026 race, which takes place on Sunday, November 1. Runners will complete 26.2 miles through New York City's five boroughs.

 ALF's marathon team is made up of runners with varying levels of experience and most have a connection to liver disease.

"ALF is grateful to once again be an official charity partner of the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon," said Lorraine Stiehl, Chief Executive Officer, American Liver Foundation. "We have an amazing group of runners who continue to raise awareness and funds for the nearly 100 million people in America affected by some form of liver disease."

All funds raised go towards ALF's mission to support those affected by liver disease. The ALF marathon team is made up of runners with varying levels of experience from novice to advanced, most of whom have a connection to liver disease.

Matthew Luneburg is the 2026 New York City Marathon Liver Life Challenge Team Captain that runs in honor of his father who is celebrating 14 years cancer-free from liver cancer. After a yearlong battle in Memphis, Tennessee that included many 2 a.m. ambulance calls and lots of tears and scary days and nights, Matthew's dad received the gift of life – a liver transplant! "Too many kids are waiting up for their mom and dad to come home. The American Liver Foundation served as a beacon of hope when that kid was me. I'll be running those 26.2 miles for them, this city, and (of course) my dad – the Spirit of New York," said Matthew Luneburg. 

Additional runners on ALF's 30-member team include: 

  • Jennie Cataldo: She's running for the first time in the NYC Marathon on Team ALF. As an Outreach Program Manager for Lahey Hospital Clinic's Division of Transplantation and Hepatobiliary Disease, Jennie understands what transplant patients go through and just wants to raise awareness of liver disease and the importance of liver transplantation.
  • Kathleen Dorfman: She's running for the first time in the NYC Marathon in honor of her nephew who was diagnosed with Biliary Atresia and received a liver transplant at 10 months old.
  • Megan Dunn: Running for the first time in the NYC Marathon, Megan has been a liver transplant and living donor social worker at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center Transplant Institute for the last four years. She wants to support her patients by raising funds for ALF that provides essential support to those with liver disease.
  • Hannah Fleming: She is running in her first marathon with Team ALF to raise awareness about liver disease. Diagnosed with Biliary Atresia, a rare liver disease, she received a life-saving liver transplant at eight months old. Today, she's a liver transplant operating room nurse who finds it incredible that she gets to work with transplant patients.
  • Kelsea Kim: Running her first NYC Marathon with Team ALF, Kelsea was diagnosed at 21 years old with Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH) and eventually primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) and ulcerative colitis (UC). She runs for those living with liver disease as well as for herself because it grounds her and lets her know her body is strong and capable.
  • Sidney Monday and Steve Nugent: They are both running for the first time in the NYC Marathon on Team ALF. Steve, a two-time liver recipient with an autoimmune liver disease, runs in honor of his amazing donors and raises awareness for organ donation. Steve has run the Boston Marathon on ALF's team for three years.
  • Saylor Smith: She's running for the first time with Team ALF in honor of her mother who lost her battle with cholangiocarcinoma after being diagnosed at 33 years old.
  • Keith Tully: He's running in the NYC marathon for the first time with Team ALF, and he has run in the Boston Marathon for 13 years with Team ALF. Tully, diagnosed with primary sclerosing cholangitis, received a lifesaving transplant from a living donor.
  • David Weston: Running in the NYC Marathon for the 3rd year on Team ALF and has run for two years in the NYC Half Marathon with Team ALF. He runs in honor of his father who exhibited so much strength in his fight against a liver disease that eventually took his life. David is inspired by his father's strength throughout his journey and has been honoring his memory for over 20 years by running in marathons.

Learn more about ALF's 2026 TCS New York City Marathon team and support their 26.2 mile run at https://liverlifechallenge.org/tcsnycmarathon/.

About the American Liver Foundation
American Liver Foundation (ALF) is a national community of patients, caregivers and medical professionals dedicated to helping people improve their liver health. Providing guidance and life-saving resources, we are a beacon for the 100 million Americans affected by liver disease. We advocate for patients and families, fund medical research, and educate the public about liver wellness and disease prevention. We bring people together through our educational programs and events and create a network of support that lasts a lifetime. ALF is the largest organization focused on all liver diseases and the trusted voice for patients and families living with liver disease. Celebrating 50 years of impact, leading the next 50 years forward. For more information, please visit www.liverfoundation.org or call: 1.800.GO.LIVER (800-465-4837).
